newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia to drop misleading accounting standards.
newsitem.headline: Russia to drop misleading accounting standards.

text.p: Russia must drop misleading accounting standards to attract foreign investment, Western accountants said on Wednesday, as a minister promised to phase out domestic audit rules to improve company efficiency.
Economy Minister Yevgeny Yasin said the government would enact a four-year plan by the end of 1996 to provide tax or other incentives for companies using international standards.

"Companies which follow these (international accounting) standards will have their profit taxes lowered by, say, five percent... or maybe they will recieve other privileges," Yasin told the American Chamber of Commerce.
Western accountants say the change is needed because Russian accounts fail to give investors the information they need.
"International investors want to see an international balance sheet so they can understand what the profits are," said a senior accountant at one of the Big Six firms in Moscow.
The problem is that Russian accounts are not even aimed at investors, said Ernst & Young banking and financial services manager Andrei Mokhov.
"Russian statutory accounting is predominantly tax driven, and as a result the economic usefulness of financial statement information is sacrificed to the taxman's needs," he said.
But analysts said the financial value of a switch to international standards varied from company to company.

"The issue is really management realising the value of producing valuable information for managing a business and investing. First the management must want to make the change," Deloitte & Touche audit partner Michael Lait said.

A Soviet institution, Russian accounting is a rule driven, form-over-substance tangle that gives managers few options on how to account for their money and produces uneven, poorly comparable reports from year to year, the analysts said.
"Russian accounts are not designed to show commercial results -- they are just a set of rules," said one Westerner.
Mokhov said results give a general view of a firm but should be used chiefly for lack of better information.

Sales figures can be used as an indication of cash flow, because of Russian firms' preference for cash accounting methods, and Russian pre-tax profit, which includes some expenses, approximates its Western equivalent, he said.
But year-on-year comparisons are distorted by inconsistently recorded information, with sales booked on a cash basis when money is received rather than when an order is placed.
"You cannot place any reliance on Russian statutory accounts as an investor," said one Western analyst.
But the government says transformation will be gradual.

"For the entire Russian economy to work by Western bookkeeping standards would require an enormous amount of work, (from) training to new forms... It cannot be solved with one decree," said government spokesman Alexander Voznesensky.
Western accountants, whose judgement plays a key role in audits, say federal authorities and Russian accountants will have to accept a new, and needed, division of power.
"Regulatory authorities are unwilling to give judgement responsiblities to the Russian accounting profession. So many areas are controlled purely by regulation," Mokhov said.
But accounting controls are desparately needed, he added.

"In certain companies, middle and upper management are not supervised or controlled either by an effective shareholders' body or internal audit. Russian accounting does not necessarily facilitate an effective control over business," he said.
"It is quite possible that a clerk may send half of the company's cash to his Swiss bank account."
